From the (N.Y.) COMMERCIAL ADVERTISER.
NUMBER VII.
To the PRESIDENT of the UNITED STATES.
THE second observation I have to make on the principles avowed in your answer, is, that the charge alleged against your predecessor, of excluding from all office those who were not of a particular sect, is not well founded.
It will be recollected that Gen. Washington, begun his administration upon the most conciliatory principles. In distributing the offices among parties, as far as they then existed, he held a most impartial hand.
When you resigned, your place was filled by Mr. Randolph, a man of the same sect. What was the consequence? Let the answer be found in the "precious confessions" which betray the secrets of government to a foreign and insidious minister...
The history of Gen. Lamb, Collector of the port of New-York, another of the same political sect with yourself, who also was found delinquent to the amount of fifty thousand dollars or more...
Another officer of the revenue in Boston, by the name of Jarvis, of the same republican sect, was guilty of a similar breach of trust...
Mr. Monroe, minister to France, another of this favorite sect, who violated his instructions, adds another example to the list of faithless public servants.
If, after all these instances of breach of confidence in the sect, which boasted of its exclusive title to republicanism, Gen. Washington, and Mr. Adams, began to question the safety of appointing pretended republicans to office, can any sober citizen blame their doubts?
But the assertion, that "by the steady pursuits of measures [exclusion] nearly all the offices were monopolized by one sect," requires great modifications to be entitled to the character of correctness.
But Gen. Washington came into office by a unanimous vote of both political events which gave a new character and direction to opposition, took place in 1793, and the subsequent years.
character. But well filled, they have been considered as permanently filled; the former Presidents never having displaced men without substantial objections to their conduct in office.
The case is precisely similar to that of a town or city incorporated, in which, at the first choice of officers, all the free citizens should agree in the choice. But in a few months one half of them, growing discontented, form a party against the officers and their adherents and exclaim most bitterly against them for a "monopoly of offices."

"THE conduct and tenor of executive and judicial appointments ought to be the subject of scrutiny. Where the appointments are bestowed upon persons of a particular way of thinking, or on the leaders of a party, we have a just right to discover from this, the drift of the administration, and as clear a privilege openly to promulge the truth, as to the facts of appointment, and to give out our opinion of the tendency of the measures.
"It has been said that the president cannot administer the government on his own principles and plans, unless his agents and servants shall coincide with him in opinions upon civil and political subjects. This assertion, in the latitude it is intended, cannot be true, or be consistent with political propriety.
